entries.narration: Python is a programming language that reads almost like English, and that is a large part of why it has become one of the most used languages in the world. On the left, Python answers three questions about itself. The version is three point fifteen point one, released this October, and it is the Python this whole course runs on. Asked to import this, it prints its own philosophy, the Zen of Python: beautiful is better than ugly, explicit is better than implicit, simple is better than complex. You will see those ideas in every piece of code in this course. And it reports that its standard library holds close to three hundred modules. That is what people mean when they say Python comes with batteries included: files, dates, JSON, CSV, databases, web servers and much more are already there, the moment you install it. On the right is what people build with it. Automation and scripts, which save hours of repetitive work. Command line tools. Web services. And data, machine learning and science, where Python has become the default. This course takes the first three, the ones every Python programmer needs, and teaches them by building one real application, from its very first line to a finished, tested, installable tool. Along the way you will learn the language properly: not just what to type, but what Python actually does with it, with short detours into how it works inside whenever a question needs the answer. Everything is standard library only, so all you need is Python itself. Here is what we will build.

Meet Ana. Like most people, she is not sure where her money goes each month. By the end of this course, she will have an app that tells her, and you will have written every line of it. This is its map. On the left are the inputs: the exports Ana downloads from her bank, messy and real, in two different text encodings, and Ana herself, typing commands. In the middle is the app, expense tracker, made of small modules, each one built in the course its label names: parsing money, reading and saving files, importing bank rows, sorting them into categories with patterns, and reporting against monthly budgets. Along the bottom are the steps that turn a working script into professional software: classes, tests, the network, and shipping it as a package with a web API. On the right is the real payoff, from the finished app, at the end of the course: October's report. Spent, budget and percentage used for every category. Fun is at a hundred and sixty percent, over budget, and transport is careful at ninety six. Every number in this course comes from really running the code, on Python three point fifteen, and nothing is typed by hand. The course has a simple rhythm. Each section adds one thing the app needs, and teaches the part of Python that does it, at exactly the moment you need it: numbers when we first handle money, dictionaries when we first need budgets, classes when the code gets big enough to need them. Let's start with an empty folder.

Every Python project starts the same way, and so does ours: an empty folder, and a Python of its own. In the terminal, we make a folder called expense tracker and step into it. Then one command, python three point fifteen, dash m, venv, dot venv, creates a virtual environment: a folder named dot venv inside the project. It prints nothing, but look at the explorer on the left. Dot venv now holds a bin folder, a lib folder, and a small file called pyvenv dot cfg, open in the editor. Its first line says where this environment came from: the Python installed in user local. Back in the terminal, the first which python answers user local. Then we activate the environment, and the same question gets a different answer: the python inside dot venv. Activating does nothing more mysterious than putting that folder first on your path. The diagram on the right shows what you really have. The environment's python is not a second copy of Python. Readlink shows it is a link to the one interpreter in user local, and it borrows that installation's standard library too. What the environment owns is its own site packages folder, where every package this project installs will go, and nowhere else. sys dot prefix points into the project, while sys dot base prefix still points at the installation it was made from. That is the whole point: two projects on one machine can need different packages, or different versions of the same package, and each keeps its own. The folder even writes its own git ignore file, so it never ends up in version control. With a Python of its own, the expense tracker is ready for its first file.

The expense tracker begins as a single file, main dot py. It is nothing more than text, four lines of it, and the explorer marks it as new. The first line starts with a hash sign, which makes it a comment: a note for people, which Python skips entirely. The second line is blank. The two lines after that are the first real code in the project, and both of them call print. In the terminal, python main dot py hands the file to the interpreter from our environment. Python reads it from the top to the bottom and runs each line in order, which is why the table on the right walks down the file one line at a time. The comment and the blank line do nothing. Line three prints the app's banner. Line four prints Ana's first expense: a coffee at Café Lumen, four fifty. Look at how that line is built, because the second table takes it apart. print was given two things, separated by a comma: some text, and a number. Text in quotes is called a string, and a number with a decimal point is called a float. print turns each of them into characters, puts a single space between them, and ends the line. Notice two things in the terminal. The quotes never appear: they only tell Python where the text starts and ends. And we typed four point five zero, but Python printed four point five. The trailing zero is gone. A float stores the number, not the way it was written, and for money that is already a warning sign. Where exactly did the zero go? To answer that, the next section follows this file through Python itself.

When you type python main dot py, Python does not run your text directly. It runs it in two phases, and this picture follows line four, the coffee, through both. Every box holds Python's own output, produced by tools that ship with it. Along the top is the compile phase. First, the source: the text we wrote. Step two splits that text into tokens, the words of the language. python dash m tokenize shows them: the name print, an opening bracket, a string, a comma, a number, a closing bracket. Notice the number token is still four point five zero, exactly as typed. Step three parses the tokens into a syntax tree, which python dash m ast prints. The line has become a call, with print as the function and two constants as its arguments. And here is the answer to the last section's puzzle: the second constant is four point five. When the parser turned the text four point five zero into a float, the zero was gone, long before print ever saw it. Step four compiles the tree into bytecode, simple instructions for Python's virtual machine, and python dash m dis lists them: load the name print, push a null, load the two constants, call with two arguments, and throw the result away. When a file is imported as a module, this bytecode is cached in the pycache folder, so the next run can skip the first three steps. Then the run phase, along the bottom. Step five is the virtual machine, which executes one instruction at a time, using a stack of values. The table shows that stack after each instruction, in CPython, the standard Python: print, then the null, then the two arguments, until call runs print and leaves its result, None. Step six is what print wrote. Every Python program you will ever run goes through this same path.

Python has a second way to run code, and it is the one you will reach for whenever you are not sure what a line will do. Typing python on its own, here with dash q to skip the banner, opens the REPL. The name describes the loop on the right: it reads the line you type, evaluates it, prints the value, and waits for the next one. Unlike a script, it shows you the value of everything, without being asked. Ana also had lunch today, twelve ninety nine, and we want the app to print what the day has cost so far. So we try it here first. Four point five zero comes straight back as four point five, the same lost zero as before. Then coffee plus lunch, four fifty plus twelve ninety nine, comes back as seventeen point four nine, followed by a long run of zeros and a two. That is not a typing mistake, and it is not a bug in Python. A float stores numbers in binary, and twelve point nine nine has no exact binary form, so what you get is the nearest value a float can hold, and the sum carries the error. The REPL is also good for small questions about text: upper turns Café Lumen into capitals, accent and all. Then exit leaves the REPL, and everything typed there is gone; the table at the bottom puts the REPL and the file side by side. Trying the line has done its job, so we write it into main dot py as line five, and run the file. The new line prints the same long number. For an app that tracks money, that is the wrong answer: amounts must come out in exact cents. We will leave it for now, deliberately, and fix it properly in the next course, with a type made for money.

Every programmer breaks their code many times a day, so one of the most useful skills you can learn is reading what Python says when it happens. Here, line five has lost its closing bracket. We run the file, and look closely at the terminal: there is no banner. Line three is perfectly correct, yet it never printed. That tells you when this error was found. You saw the path in the last picture but one: before Python runs a single line, it parses the whole file, checking its grammar, every bracket closed and every colon in place. The diagram on the right follows that path. The parser reached the end of the file with a bracket still open, so it stopped, and nothing ran at all. Now read the error itself, line by line, with the table beside it. The first line names the file and the line number, five. The second line shows that line of code. The third line has a caret pointing up, at the bracket that was opened and never closed. And the last line says what kind of error this is, a SyntaxError, followed by a plain description: the opening bracket was never closed. Python's messages have become far more helpful in recent versions, and this one says exactly what is wrong. Notice that the caret points at where the bracket was opened, not at where the missing one belongs. For a missing bracket, the true mistake is often at the end of the line, or even on a later line. So the habit is: read the last line of the error first, then the line it points at, then look around it. Next, an error that the parser cannot see.

This time the bracket is back, but on line four, print has been typed as p r n t. As far as the parser is concerned, that is perfectly good Python: p r n t is a valid name, so the file passes the grammar check and starts running. The table on the right shows what happened, line by line. Line three runs, and the banner appears in the terminal. Then line four runs, and Python has to find out what p r n t means. It looks in two places, shown in the diagram: the names this file has defined, and then the built in names that every program starts with, such as print and len. Neither has anything called p r n t, so Python raises a NameError, and line five never runs. The traceback reads the same way as before. It gives the file and the line, underlines the name it could not find, and on the last line names the error and adds a suggestion: did you mean print? Python suggests a close match whenever it can find one, and it is usually right. The table at the bottom is the real lesson of this pair. A SyntaxError is found by the parser, before any line runs, so nothing happens at all. A NameError is found by the running program, only when it reaches the bad line, so everything before that line has already happened. Here that means one printed banner. In an app that saves your expenses, it could mean a file half written, which is why this course will check its input, and test its code, before it trusts either. Fix the name, and the project is set up. In the next course, it starts to hold real data.

An expense tracker has to remember things, so this course is about how Python holds data, starting with the simplest piece: a name. In main dot py, Ana's first expense is now four names: the date, a description, an amount and a category. The table on the right lists them. Each line is an assignment, and an assignment does not put a value into a box. It binds a name to an object, and the object lives in an area of memory called the heap. That difference sounds academic, so the REPL makes it concrete. We bind amount to four fifty, then bind paid to amount. Now both names refer to the same object, which the top diagram draws as two arrows meeting at one float. Then we give amount a new value, five twenty. Did paid change? The REPL says no: paid is still four point five. The lower diagram shows why. Assignment made a new float object and moved only amount's arrow; paid kept pointing at the old one. The is operator asks whether two names refer to the same object, and now it answers False. Keep this picture in mind, names as arrows to objects, because it explains almost every surprise later in this course: why one change can show up in two places, and why another change shows up in only one. Next, we look closely at one of these objects, the amount, because for money a float is the wrong kind of number.

In the first course, coffee plus lunch came out as seventeen point four nine, followed by a long tail of digits. Here is the smallest version of that problem: zero point one plus zero point two, which Python says is zero point three, followed by zeros and a four. A float stores numbers in binary, with a fixed number of bits, and most decimal fractions, like a tenth, have no exact binary form. The top table shows what is really stored for zero point one: Decimal of the float reveals every digit of the nearest value the float can hold. For measuring a distance, that tiny error is harmless. For money it is not, because errors add up, and a total that is off by a fraction of a cent will not match a bank statement. Python's standard library has a type made for this, Decimal, from the decimal module. Built from a string, Decimal of zero point one is exactly one tenth, and zero point one plus zero point two is exactly zero point three. In main dot py, the amount and the lunch become Decimals, built from strings, and today's total prints as seventeen forty nine, cents and all. Notice that the coffee now prints as four fifty, with its zero: a Decimal keeps the precision you gave it. The bottom table is the rule this course follows. An int counts things, a float measures things approximately, and a Decimal holds money exactly. One trap to remember: always build a Decimal from a string. Building it from a float copies the float's error along with it.

Most of the data in an expense tracker is text: dates, shop names, categories. In Python, text is a string, and a string is a sequence of characters, each with a position called its index. The top table lays out the date, two thousand twenty six, dash, ten, dash, zero one, one character per cell. Indexes start at zero, and they also count backwards from the end, starting at minus one. That makes slicing easy. A slice takes a start and a stop, and the stop is not included. Date from five to seven is the month, ten. Date from minus two to the end is the day, zero one. Date up to seven, which main dot py now uses, is the year and month together, the key Ana's monthly reports will group by. The middle diagram draws each slice and the new string it produces. That word, new, matters. Strings never change. A slice, or upper, which main dot py uses to print the shop's name in capitals, accent and all, builds a new string and leaves the original exactly as it was. The other new idea in this step is the f string. Put an f before the quotes, and any name in curly braces is replaced by its value. The bottom table shows three of them and what they printed. F strings are the clearest way to build a line of output from data, and they will carry the report we build later, where we will also control widths and alignment. For now, one expense prints as a tidy line.

Real data has gaps, and an expense tracker has to tell different kinds of gap apart. Take a note on an expense. Sometimes there is a note. Sometimes we asked Ana, and she left it blank. And sometimes we never asked at all. Those are three different states, drawn on the right. For the second one, Python has None, a single object that means: there is no value here. For the third, Python three point fifteen adds a new built in, sentinel. A sentinel is a unique marker you create and name yourself, here not asked, which can never be confused with None or with real data. In main dot py, the note is None and the receipt is not asked. To test for either, use is, not double equals: is asks whether this is that exact object, and there is only one None, and only one not asked. The first printed line answers both questions: there is no note, and the receipt was never asked for. Why not just test whether the note is truthy? The REPL shows the danger. None is falsy, but so are zero, the empty string and the empty list. If a missing value and a zero amount both look False, a refund of nothing and a missing amount become the same thing. So test for None with is, and test for a sentinel with is. You will meet sentinels again when we write functions, where the difference between not given and given as None really matters.

One expense is not a tracker. Ana's day had three, and Python's most common way to hold many things in order is a list. A list is written in square brackets, and main dot py's today starts with two amounts, the coffee and the lunch. Then append adds the metro ride to the end. Look at the diagram. The list is one object with three numbered slots, and each slot refers to an object, exactly as a name does. The first slot and the name amount point at the very same four fifty, so a list does not copy what you put in it; it refers to it. In the REPL, we try the operations on a list of words. Indexing works as it did for strings: zero is the first item and minus one is the last. A slice returns a new list, here lunch and metro. Unlike a string, a list can change: append grew it, and it can also shrink, be sorted, or have a slot replaced. Back in main dot py, two built in functions answer the questions an expense tracker asks most often. len counts the items, three, and sum adds them up: twenty twenty nine, exact, because every item is a Decimal. That is the first real total our app has computed. But these are bare amounts. We no longer know which one was the coffee, or what category the metro belongs to. Each expense has several fields that belong together, and the next section gives them a shape.

An expense is a small record: a date, a description, an amount and a category. Python's simplest way to keep fields like these together is a tuple, written with round brackets and commas. In main dot py, today is now a list of three tuples, one per expense. The list holds many things of one kind; each tuple holds the fixed fields of one thing. The table in the middle puts that rule side by side. The next line uses one of Python's most useful features, unpacking. Four names on the left of the equals sign, one tuple on the right, and Python assigns the fields in order: the date to date, the description to description, and so on. The diagram draws each field of today zero going to its name. Unpacking replaces four separate lines of indexing, and it fails loudly if the count does not match, which catches mistakes early. The terminal prints the first expense the same way as before, and three expenses today. The REPL shows the other half of what makes a tuple a tuple. We make a small expense and try to change its description to bus. Python refuses with a TypeError: a tuple does not support item assignment. That is a feature, not a limitation. A record that cannot change by accident is a record you can share freely. If Ana's metro ride really was a bus, we build a new tuple, and the old one is untouched. Next, a container where we look things up by name instead of by position.

Ana wants a budget for each category: three hundred for food, eighty for transport, sixty for fun, and nine fifty for rent. That is a mapping from a name to a value, and Python's tool for it is the dictionary, written with curly braces and key colon value pairs. In main dot py, budgets is a dict with three categories, and the next line adds rent by assigning to a new key. Reading a budget is the same square bracket syntax, with a key instead of a position: budgets of food is three hundred. How does Python find food without searching? The diagram shows the idea. It calls hash on the key, which turns the string into a number, and that number picks a slot in a table, so one hash leads straight to the value, however many categories Ana adds. Every string, int and tuple can be hashed, which is why they can be dict keys. The exact slot numbers change from run to run for strings, so the diagram shows the idea, not real slots. Now the REPL, with python dash i, which runs main dot py and then keeps its names for us to explore. Asking for a category that does not exist, gifts, with square brackets, raises a KeyError, which the traceback names exactly. When a missing key is normal, use get, with a default: budgets dot get gifts, zero, quietly answers zero. Square brackets when the key must be there, get when it might not. Dicts also remember the order keys were added, which keeps reports predictable.

Two more containers complete the set, and both are about rules. The first is the set itself. Which categories did Ana use today? Collect the category of each expense into a set, and duplicates disappear: food appears twice in the day, but the set keeps it once, as the diagram shows. Sets are also built for one question, is this in it, which they answer with a single hash, like a dict. The catch is that a set has no order. The order you see can even change between runs, so main dot py sorts it before printing: food and transport. Has Ana spent on fun today? The in operator says False. The second container is new in Python three point fifteen: frozendict, a dictionary that cannot be changed. The app's default budgets are now a frozendict, a single source of truth, and Ana's working budgets are a normal dict copied from it, which she is free to edit. In the REPL, we try to change the default for fun, and Python refuses with a TypeError, just as it did for a tuple. Nothing in the program can change the defaults by accident, whatever goes wrong elsewhere. The middle table is a summary worth pausing on. Lists and tuples keep order and allow duplicates; one can change, one cannot. Dicts map keys to values and remember their order. Sets keep each thing once, in no order. And frozendict is a dict that is frozen. Choosing the right container is half of writing clear code.

This last section of the course returns to names and arrows, because they explain the most common bug in Python. main dot py now holds a month, october, a dict that maps each day to its list of expenses. In the REPL, we make two copies of it. copy dot copy makes a shallow copy: a new dict, whose values refer to the same objects as the original's. deepcopy makes a deep copy: a new dict, and new copies of everything inside it. Then Ana remembers a bakery stop and appends it to today. How many expenses does each copy now hold? The shallow copy says four, the deep copy says three. The diagram shows why. October and shallow are two different dicts, but both of their arrows lead to the one list, today, so a change to the list shows up in both. Only the deep copy has a list of its own, still holding three expenses. When two names lead to one mutable object, that is called aliasing, and it is the source of countless surprises. The rule is simple: copying a container copies its slots, not what they refer to. The last line shows how CPython keeps track of all these arrows. Every object carries a reference count, the number of references to it. sys dot getrefcount of today says four: the name today, the october dict, the shallow copy, and the temporary reference getrefcount's own argument makes. When a count drops to zero, CPython frees the object at once. The app now holds a day of expenses and its budgets. Next, it learns to make decisions about them.

The app now holds data. This course teaches it to work with that data: to calculate, to decide, to repeat, and to react to what Ana types. We start by tidying main dot py. The experiments from the last course are gone, and what remains is the app's data: the budgets, frozen, and a week of Ana's expenses, seven tuples long. Then three lines of arithmetic answer a real question: how is transport going? Spent is the metro plus the train to Porto, seventy one twenty. Left is the budget minus that, eight eighty. And used is the share of the budget gone, as a percentage. Each of those lines is an expression, and Python evaluates an expression by precedence, then left to right. The REPL shows the rules. Two plus three times four is fourteen, because multiplication comes before addition, and brackets change the order, giving twenty. Two star star ten is a power, one thousand and twenty four. Python has three kinds of division, in the second table: a single slash gives the true result, three and a half; a double slash gives the whole number of times, three; and percent gives the remainder, one. On the right, the diagram walks through the used line. Division and multiplication have the same rank, so Python goes left to right: seventy one twenty divided by eighty first, then times a hundred. Rounding to one place, the terminal reports eighty nine percent used. That number is close to the limit, and the app should say so. To do that, it needs to make a decision.

A budget tracker is only useful if it tells Ana something: over budget, careful, or on track. Each is a decision, and Python writes decisions with if, elif and else. Read the new lines in main dot py as plain English. If more than a hundred percent is used, say over budget, by how much. Otherwise, if eighty percent or more is used, say careful, and how much is left. Otherwise, say on track. The colon at the end of each test, and the indented line under it, mark the block that belongs to that branch. The diagram on the right lights the path Python took for transport at eighty nine percent. Is it more than a hundred? No, so the first branch is skipped. Is it eighty or more? Yes, so the careful line prints, and the else is skipped entirely. That is the rule worth remembering: Python checks the tests from the top and runs the first branch whose test is true, and only that one. So the order matters. If the eighty percent test came first, an over budget category would be reported as merely careful. The REPL shows what the tests themselves are: comparisons, which answer True or False. Used greater than a hundred is False, used at least eighty is True. Python also lets you chain comparisons the way you would write them in maths, so eighty is less than or equal to used is less than or equal to a hundred reads naturally, and answers True. The terminal says it plainly: transport, careful, eight eighty left. But that is one category, added up by hand. Next, a loop does it for all of them.

Adding up transport by picking out two items by position does not scale: Ana will have hundreds of expenses, and positions change. What we need is to visit every expense once, and that is what a for loop does. The first loop in main dot py reads: for each expense in the list, unpack it into four names, and add its amount to the running total for its category. The table on the right follows it pass by pass. On the first pass, the names are bound to the coffee, and food's total becomes four fifty. On the second, they are rebound to the noodle bar, and food reaches seventeen forty nine. The loop never copies the list; it moves a cursor down it and rebinds the same four names each time, until the seventh pass, the concert tickets, pushes fun to seventy five fifty. Notice how the running totals start. The first time a category appears, there is no total yet, so get with a default of zero supplies one. Then a second loop walks the totals dict itself. items gives each category with its total, and the decision from the last section runs once per category, now written with f strings. The terminal shows the three answers the diagram connects to their totals: food is on track, with two hundred thirty six thirty one left; transport is careful; and fun is over budget by fifteen fifty. Those concert tickets did it. Two short loops and a decision have turned a list of expenses into a budget report. Next, the app starts listening to Ana.

So far, main dot py runs from top to bottom and stops. A real tool waits for you, does what you ask, and waits again. That shape is a loop that does not walk a collection: a while loop, which repeats as long as its condition is true. While True repeats forever, until something inside it says stop. Inside, input prints the prompt, expense, and waits for Ana to type a line, which it returns as a string. Then come the loop's two exits, drawn on the right. If the command is quit, break leaves the loop at once, and the program ends. If the command is anything but report, the app prints the commands it knows, and continue jumps straight back to the top of the loop, skipping the rest of the body. Only when the command is report does the body reach the report, which is the same code as before, now indented one level inside the loop. In the terminal, you can follow a real session. Ana types help, and gets the list of commands, through the continue. She types report, and the three budget lines appear, followed by the prompt again: the loop came round. She types quit, and the program ends. The table at the bottom traces each line to the path it took. Notice that break and continue are about the loop, not about if: they work from anywhere inside the loop's body. With a loop that listens, the app has become an interactive tool. Next, it needs to understand more than one word at a time.

Ana wants to add an expense from the prompt: add, nine eighty, fun. That command has three parts, and comparing whole strings will not do. Python's match statement was designed for exactly this. split breaks the line into a list of words, and match compares that list against each case, from the top. Each case is a pattern, not a value. The first pattern is a list of three items whose first item is the word add; the other two are names, amount and category, and if the pattern matches, they are bound to whatever words were there. The diagram on the right lines up this session's commands with the case each one matched. Add nine eighty fun has three words starting with add, so the first case matches, and the table below it shows the names it bound: amount is the string nine eighty, and category is fun. The app makes a Decimal from the amount and appends a new expense. Report is a list of one word, so it matches the report case, and the report runs. Notice that a list pattern checks the length too: report on its own matches, but report with an extra word would not. Quit matches its own case and breaks out of the loop. And the final case, an underscore, matches anything at all, so every unknown command gets the help text. The report proves the add worked: fun is now over budget by twenty five thirty, nine eighty more than before. One problem is visible already: typing a word that is not a number as the amount would crash the app. We will deal with that before this course ends.

Two common jobs in this app are filtering, keeping only some expenses, and totalling, adding some of them up. Python has a compact way to write both: comprehensions. The new list command needs the expenses of one category. In main dot py it is a single line: a list of e, for each e in expenses, if its category matches. Read it from the middle: for each expense, if it is in the category, keep it. The diagram on the right lines up its parts with the loop it stands for: the for clause is the loop, the if clause is the test inside it, and the e at the front is what gets appended. A comprehension is not magic; it is that loop, written as an expression. The report has also become shorter. Instead of a running total in a dict, each category's spending is one call to sum, given a generator expression: the same shape in round brackets, which produces the values one at a time instead of building a list. Every category, rent included, is now reported, even with nothing spent. In the terminal, list food prints the three food expenses. The REPL shows something new in Python three point fifteen: unpacking in comprehensions. Days is a list of lists. Star day, for each day in days, unpacks each inner list into the result, giving one flat list: coffee, lunch, metro. Before three fifteen this needed two for clauses. Comprehensions are a good habit while they stay readable: a filter and a transformation. When the logic needs more than one test or a temporary name, write the loop.

The loop in main dot py has been growing, with the report written out in full inside one of its cases. It is time to give pieces of the app names. A function is a named block of code that takes inputs, called parameters, and returns a value. main dot py now has three. total takes a category and returns what was spent on it. status takes a category and its budget, calls total, and returns the sentence for the report. And report loops over the budgets and prints each status. The loop's report case is now one line: report. The code reads as what it does. Every time a function is called, Python creates a frame: a small workspace holding that call's own names. The diagram on the right freezes the moment inside total, while it adds up transport. At the bottom is the module's frame, holding the names of main dot py itself: expenses and the budgets. report was called, so its frame sits on top, with its category and budget. report called status, which pushed another frame, and status called total, at the top of the stack. Each frame has its own category name, and they never clash. When total reaches return, its frame is popped off the stack, and seventy one twenty goes back to status, which builds its sentence and returns it to report, which prints it. This stack of frames is called the call stack, and you have already seen it printed: a traceback is the call stack at the moment something went wrong. The terminal shows the result: the same report, rent now included, from three small functions.

You have now seen both halves of how Python uses memory, separately: names pointing at objects, and frames on the call stack. This picture puts them together, using a small lab file that runs the same pattern as our report. On the left is the stack, top first. When the program is inside total, there are three frames: total, report, and the module. That list is real: it is what Python's inspect module returned, printed in the terminal below the stack. Each frame holds names, and nothing else. Total's frame holds exactly two, category and frames, which Python's own frame object reported. Report's frame has a name, spent, waiting for total to return. The module's frame holds the program's global names: the expenses list, and the two functions. On the right is the heap, where every object lives: the string food, the list of frame names, the expenses list, the tuple inside it, and the function objects themselves, because in Python a function is an object too. Every arrow is a reference. A name refers to an object; a slot in a list refers to an object. And every object carries a reference count, the number of references to it. The lab printed the list's count from inside total: two. One is the module's name, expenses, and one is the temporary reference made by passing it to getrefcount. When a function returns, its frame is popped, and its names disappear. Any object whose count falls to zero is freed at once, in CPython. Names live in frames, frames live on the stack, and objects live on the heap. Every Python program you will read follows this one model.

Adding an expense deserves a function of its own, and it is a good place to learn how arguments really work. add underscore expense takes four parameters. The first two, amount and category, are required. The last two have defaults: a description, added by hand, and a date. A caller can pass arguments by position, in order, or by keyword, with name equals value, and any parameter it leaves out takes its default. The add case now captures any extra words with star words, joins them into a note, and passes it as the description. In the terminal, add three twenty, food, bakery near work, binds the four parameters as the table shows: the amount, the category and the description by position, and the date from its default. The function returns the new count of expenses, eight. Defaults hide one of Python's best known traps, and the REPL demonstrates it. A small function, tag, has a default of an empty list, and appends a word to it. The first call returns bakery, as expected. The second call, with metro, returns bakery and metro. The diagram shows why. A default is created once, when the def line runs, not each time the function is called. Both calls received the same list object, and the first call's word was still in it. So the rule is: never use a mutable object, such as a list or a dict, as a default. Use None, and create a fresh list inside the function when the argument is None. That is exactly why None, the value from the last course, appears in so many function signatures.

Ana would like to know how many expenses she added this session, so main dot py gains a counter, added, starting at zero, and add underscore expense adds one to it. There is also a new setting, warn at, eighty, which status now uses instead of a bare number. Let us run it. Ana adds a bakery visit, and the app crashes with an UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable added, where it is not associated with a value. But added is right there at the top of the file. To understand why, you need Python's scope rules, drawn on the right. When code uses a name, Python looks in four places, in order: the local scope of the function that is running, then any enclosing functions, then the global scope of the module, then the built ins. That is called L E G B. Status reads warn at, which is not local, so Python finds it in the global scope, and that works fine. Add underscore expense is different, because it assigns to added. Any name that a function assigns to is treated as local everywhere in that function, so added plus equals one means: add one to the local added. And the local added has no value yet. The rules table puts the two cases side by side: reading a global just works; assigning to one makes a new local. The fix, in the next step, is one line: global added, which tells Python that this function means the module's name. Use global sparingly. A function that changes module names is harder to reason about, which is why the app will eventually keep its state inside an object.

The app has a weakness we noticed when match arrived: any text typed as an amount went straight into Decimal. This last section makes the app react to bad input instead of crashing. First, global added fixes the scope bug from the last section. Then main dot py defines its own exception, InvalidAmount, a class that is a kind of ValueError. You will learn classes properly later; for now, this two line class gives a specific kind of error a name. A new function, parse amount, does the checking. It tries to make a Decimal; if the text is not a number, Decimal raises InvalidOperation, which parse amount catches and replaces with our own InvalidAmount, with a clear message. If the number is zero or negative, it raises InvalidAmount itself. And in the add case, try runs the risky call, except catches an InvalidAmount and prints why the expense was not added, and else runs only when nothing went wrong. Look at the session. Ana types twelve comma fifty, the way amounts are written in much of Europe, and the app says it is not a number, and carries on. She types minus three, and it says the amount must be more than zero. Then twelve fifty is added. The diagram shows the path the exception took: raised in parse amount's frame, it travelled up the call stack, frame by frame, until the loop's except clause caught it. Had nothing caught it, it would have reached the top, and you would have seen a traceback. That is the shape of robust code: check early, raise a specific error, and handle it where you can say something useful. The app can decide, repeat and react. Next, it learns to remember.

Everything the app knows disappears when Ana types quit. To remember, it has to write to a file, and this course is about files: writing them, reading them, and trusting what is in them. The app has also lost its starting banner, to keep the terminal for what matters. A new command, save, calls save text, which opens a file named expenses dot txt for writing and writes one line per expense, fields separated by a bar. The key word is with. open returns a file object, and a file must be closed when you are done, or the last of your data may never reach the disk. with guarantees that: when the block ends, the file is closed, whatever happened inside it. The diagram on the right shows the three steps, and the first table shows why with matters. If a write fails halfway, without with the file is left open and half written; with with, it is closed, and the error carries on up to whoever can handle it. open's second argument is the mode: r to read, which is the default, w to write, which replaces the file, and a to append to its end. In the terminal, save reports seven expenses, and head shows the first three lines of the file, exactly as written, café and all. The data now outlives the program. But look at what was lost. In the file, four fifty is just four characters again; the Decimal has gone, along with the fact that the date is a date. To read this file back, we would have to split each line and rebuild every type by hand. There is a standard format that does most of that for us.

JSON is a text format for structured data, and almost every system in the world can read and write it: browsers, databases, other languages. Python's json module converts between JSON and Python's own types. The diagram on the right is the mapping. A list becomes a JSON array, a dict becomes a JSON object, and a string stays a string. Our expenses are tuples, so save first turns each one into a dict with named fields, which makes the file self describing. Then json dot dump writes them, indented so a person can read it, and with ensure ascii off so café stays café. There is one type JSON does not have: Decimal. JSON's numbers become floats when read back, and we have spent a whole course keeping floats away from money. So this is a decision, and it is ours to make: the amount is saved as a string, four fifty in quotes, and load turns it back into a Decimal. The code panel on the right shows the start of the real file. load does the reverse of save, and the app now calls it at startup. The first time, there is no file yet, so open raises FileNotFoundError, which the app catches, starting from the sample week instead. The terminal proves the round trip. In the first run, Ana adds snacks, saves eight expenses, and quits. In the second run, a brand new process, list fun shows the cinema, the concert, and the snacks: loaded back from the file. The app finally remembers.

The project is about to have more files, so it needs a proper place for them. In the explorer there is a new folder, data. It holds the expenses file, and a bank folder with two exports Ana has downloaded from her bank, one for September and one for October. Working with paths as plain strings gets messy fast, so Python has pathlib, whose Path objects know how paths work. In the REPL, a path is built with the slash operator: data, slash bank, slash the file name. Python uses the right separator for your system, so the same code works on Windows. A Path has parts, drawn on the right: its parent folder, its name, the stem without the extension, and the suffix. In main dot py, three constants now describe where everything lives: DATA, the expenses file inside it, and the BANK folder. Saving and loading use the Path's own open method, and since the expenses file now exists, the app always loads it. The sample week has gone from the code: the data lives in data, where it belongs. A new command, exports, uses glob, which finds every file in a folder that matches a pattern, here star dot csv. sorted puts them in order, and for each one, stat reports facts about the file, such as its size. The terminal lists both exports, two hundred and five bytes for September and four hundred and thirty seven for October. The app can find Ana's bank data. Before it can use that data, it has to read it, and the September file is about to cause trouble.

A file on disk does not contain text. It contains bytes, numbers from zero to two hundred and fifty five, and text is those bytes decoded with an encoding: a rule for which bytes mean which characters. For English letters, almost every encoding agrees. For a letter like E with an accent, they do not. In the REPL, we read the September export as raw bytes, with mode r b, and try to decode it the way Python three point fifteen does by default: as UTF-8. It fails, with a UnicodeDecodeError: byte C nine, at position forty seven, is an invalid continuation byte. The diagram shows what happened. In UTF-8, an accented capital E is two bytes. But Ana's old bank app saved this file in Latin-1, where it is the single byte C nine. Decoded as Latin-1, the same bytes read correctly: CAFÉ MÜLLER. The table in the middle explains why this matters more in three fifteen. Until now, open used your operating system's encoding, which differed between machines, so the same program could read a file on one computer and fail on another. Python three fifteen makes UTF-8 the default everywhere, so the behaviour is predictable, and files in other encodings fail loudly instead of silently. main dot py now has read export, which tries UTF-8 first and falls back to Latin-1. The order is not arbitrary: Latin-1 can decode any bytes at all, so it never fails, and it would happily turn a UTF-8 file into nonsense. Always try the strict encoding first. You will see read export at work in the next section.

Bank exports are CSV files: comma separated values, a table as plain text, one row per line, with a header line naming the columns. It is tempting to read CSV by splitting each line on commas, but look at line nine of the October export: an amount written as twelve comma fifty, in quotes. The quotes mean it is one field. Splitting on commas would cut it in two and shift every column after it. The csv module knows the real rules, quotes included. Its DictReader is the most useful tool in it. It reads the header, then turns every following line into a dict whose keys are the column names. The terminal's first command prints the first row of the October export that way, and the diagram on the right draws the mapping: each header cell becomes a key, and the line's fields become the values. That makes code readable: row of amount, not row of two. In main dot py, read rows reads an export's text with read export, from the last section, and hands its lines to DictReader. The new import command reads both files and reports what it found: five rows from the September file, read correctly in Latin-1, and twelve from October, with the same four columns. Notice one thing in the diagram: the amount is a string. CSV has no types at all, so every value arrives as text, and nothing has been checked. A missing date, a currency the app cannot handle, an amount that is not a number: all of them are just strings so far. Before any of this goes into Ana's expenses, the app has to decide which rows to trust.

Data from outside the program is never trusted until it has been checked. This section adds the check, and its rule is simple: keep the good rows, report the bad ones with a reason, and never stop silently. A new exception, InvalidRow, names what can go wrong with a bank row. validate runs the checks in the order drawn on the right. Is there a date? Is the amount in pounds, the only currency the app understands so far? Is the amount a positive number? That one reuses parse amount from the last course, with all its checks. And has this exact expense been seen before? Each check raises an error if it fails. A row that passes every check becomes an expense, with the category other for now. import bank keeps a set of what it has seen, starting with the expenses already saved, so importing twice does not double everything. For each row, it tries validate. Both InvalidRow and InvalidAmount are kinds of ValueError, so a single except clause catches either, and prints the file, the line number and the reason. enumerate counts the lines, starting at two, because line one is the header. The terminal shows the result. September imports cleanly, five rows. October imports seven and rejects five, and the table lists them: the second Pret a Manger on the same day, a duplicate. Twelve comma fifty. A row with no date. A refund, which is not an expense. And forty eight euros, which needs an exchange rate, something the app will learn to fetch later. Every rejected row is visible. Ana's data now comes from her bank, but most of it is filed under other. Next, the app learns to sort it.

Twelve of Ana's expenses came from the bank, and every one of them is filed under other, because a bank does not know what a payment was for. All it gives us is a description: AMZN MKTP UK star two K four, TFL TRAVEL CH, THAMES WATER. Recognising text like that is the job of regular expressions, a small pattern language that Python provides in the re module. main dot py now has RULES, a list of pairs: a compiled pattern and the category it means. The table in the middle explains the three pieces of the language these patterns use. A caret anchors the match to the start of the text, so caret AMZN MKTP only matches a description that begins that way. A vertical bar means or, so TESCO bar PRET matches either. Square brackets mean any one of these characters, so CAF, then E or E acute, matches CAFE and CAFÉ. categorise tries the rules in order and returns the first category whose pattern is found anywhere in the description, or other if none is. The diagram on the right shows five real descriptions and where they landed. A new command, categorise, goes through the expenses that are still other and files them, and from now on, every import is categorised as it arrives. In the terminal, categorise files all twelve, list shopping finds the Amazon order, and save keeps the result. Then the REPL, which python dash i opens once the app quits, shows a match object, the part of the text that matched, and categorise sending a bakery to other. The rules are data: teaching the app a new shop means adding one line, not changing any logic.

Back in the decisions course, the report added up each category by walking the whole list once per category. With six categories and hundreds of expenses, that is a lot of walking for an answer we can get in one pass. The collections module has two tools made for grouping. The first is defaultdict. Normally, adding to a key that does not exist yet raises a KeyError. A defaultdict is given a function that makes a starting value, here Decimal, which returns zero, so the first time a category is touched, it is created with a total of zero, and plus equals simply works. The diagram shows the expenses dropping into their buckets, and shopping appearing on first touch. spent by category builds every total in a single loop, and report looks each one up. The second tool is Counter, a dict made for counting. Give it any collection, here every description, and it counts how often each appears. most common three returns the top three, and the new payees command prints them: TFL travel, three times, then Netflix and Thames Water, twice each. Now look at the report, because it has a problem. Transport is over budget by two forty, and fun by forty seven. But those totals add September's spending to October's, and the budgets are monthly. The app has never needed to know what month an expense belongs to. It will, two sections from now. First, a smaller improvement: putting things in order.

A report is easier to read when the biggest numbers come first. Python's built in sorted function takes any collection and returns a new, sorted list, leaving the original exactly as it was. Sorted can compare numbers and strings on its own, but our expenses are tuples, and we want them in order of their amount. That is what the key argument is for. key is a function: sorted calls it once on every item, and sorts by whatever it returns. The function here is tiny, so it is written inline as a lambda: lambda e, colon, e two. A lambda is a function with no name and a single expression for its body, which it returns. reverse equals True puts the biggest first. The new top command sorts the expenses by amount and prints the first three: the train to Porto, the concert tickets, and the Corner Market shop. The report uses the same idea with a different key. Instead of the budgets' own order, it sorts the categories by how much was spent in each, biggest first, using a lambda that looks up the category's total. The plot on the right draws those totals in that order: food, fun, transport, bills, shopping, and rent, with nothing spent. These are still both months together, which the next section fixes. One habit worth taking from this section: when you need an order, pass sorted a key that says what to compare, rather than rearranging the data to suit it.

Budgets are monthly, so the app has to understand dates, and Python's datetime module is how it does. A date object knows the calendar: months of different lengths, leap years, all of it. Subtract two dates and you get a timedelta, a length of time, and you can add or subtract a timedelta to move a date. The REPL shows both. Thirty days before the sixteenth of October is the sixteenth of September. And the Netflix payments, on the ninth of September and the ninth of October, are thirty days apart. In main dot py, TODAY is a fixed date, the sixteenth of October. A real app would ask the system for today's date, but this course fixes it, so that every run of every example gives the same answer. Our dates are stored as text in the form year, month, day, and that format was chosen on purpose: it sorts correctly as text, and its first seven characters are the month. So spent by category now takes a month, and only adds expenses whose date starts with it. report with no argument means this month, and report with a month shows that one instead. recent uses real date arithmetic: it turns each stored date into a date object with fromisoformat, and keeps those after a date a number of days ago. Recent seven finds two expenses, the metro and the water bill, thirty five twenty. The plot on the right is October, day by day, from Ana's own data: the train and the concert stand out on the fourth and the fifth. The report finally means what Ana thinks it means.

Subscriptions and bills are the expenses people forget about, because they never decide to pay them again. The app can find them by putting together what this course has taught so far. A recurring payment has the same payee, the same amount, and comes about a month apart. recurring follows the three steps drawn on the right. First, it groups: a defaultdict of lists collects every date for each pair of payee and amount. Second, it measures: the dates are sorted, and zip pairs each date with the next one, so subtracting them gives the gap between payments, in days. Third, it decides: if there is at least one gap, and every gap is between twenty five and thirty five days, the payment is recurring. The all function makes that check read like the sentence. Notice that recurring does not build a list of results. It uses yield, which hands back one result at a time to the loop that is asking for them. The terminal shows what it found in Ana's data: Netflix, ten ninety nine, thirty days apart, and the Thames Water bill, thirty two forty, also thirty days apart. The second table shows two near misses, and why they were rejected. TFL appears in both months, but the amounts differ: those are separate journeys. The Tesco shop also appears twice, but for very different amounts. Rules like these will never be perfect, but they are clear, and anyone can read why a payment was flagged. That word yield is worth a closer look, and the next section takes it.

A function that contains yield is a generator function, and calling it does not run it. The REPL shows this. bank rows reads every bank export, but calling it returns instantly: the result is a generator object, and not a single file has been opened yet. Each time you call next on the generator, the function runs until it reaches yield, hands back that value, and pauses, keeping its whole frame: its local names, and exactly where it stopped. The diagram on the right shows that paused frame, holding the current path, line number and row. The first next returns the first row of the September file, Café Müller. The second resumes from where the first stopped, and returns line three. Then a generator expression counts the rest: fifteen more. Asked again, the generator would be empty, because a generator can only be walked once. Why does this matter? Look at what import bank used to do: read every file into a list of rows, then walk the list. A generator never holds more than one row at a time. With two small exports, the difference is invisible; with a year of exports from several accounts, it is the difference between a program that streams through its data and one that needs it all in memory at once. And the code reads better too: bank rows owns the question of where rows come from, including both encodings, and import bank only decides what to do with each row, now with the file name and line number it was handed. A for loop calls next for you, which is why every loop you have written so far has worked on generators without you noticing.

The report says the right things now, but as loose sentences. This last section of the course turns it into a table you can read at a glance. f strings can do more than insert a value: after the name, a colon introduces a format specification, a short code for how the value should look. The diagram takes one apart: spent, colon, greater than, nine, point two, f. Greater than means align right, nine is the width in characters, point two means two decimal places, and f means show it as a fixed point number. Right alignment is what makes a column of numbers line up on the decimal point. The other specifications in status work the same way. category with less than ten is left aligned, ten wide. The bar is a string of hash signs, one for every ten percent used, up to ten, padded to ten characters so the percentages line up after it. And used, with point zero f, is a whole percentage. A conditional expression picks the flag: over, careful, or nothing. report prints a header line, built with the same specifications so the titles sit above their columns. The terminal shows October. Fun is at a hundred and sixty percent, a full bar, flagged over. Transport is at ninety six, careful. Food is at thirty one, and rent shows zero, printed as zero point zero zero, because the f format pads every amount to two places. The app has grown from one printed line to a working tool, all in a single file, now well over two hundred lines long. That is the problem the next course solves.

main dot py has grown past two hundred lines, and finding anything in it means scrolling. Every Python file is also a module, something another file can import, so the cure is to split it by subject. The explorer shows the result: five new modules. money holds the amount parsing. store knows where the data lives and how to read and write it. categorise has the rules, bank imports exports, and report owns the budgets, the dates and the monthly table. main dot py keeps only the command loop, about seventy lines, and starts by importing what it needs. One thing had to change along the way. Each module has its own global names, so a function in report cannot see main's expenses list. Functions now take the expenses as an argument, which also makes it obvious what each one works on. What does import actually do? The first time a module is imported, Python runs it, top to bottom, and stores the result in a dictionary called sys dot modules, so a second import is just a lookup. Python three point fifteen adds a choice: lazy import. Only the import command needs the bank module, so main dot py imports it lazily. The name bank exists, but the module is not loaded until something uses it. The REPL proves it. After the app quits, report is in sys dot modules, and bank is not. Then we touch bank dot InvalidRow, the module loads at that moment, and now bank is there too. For a small app, this saves little; for a command line tool that imports heavy libraries, it can make startup feel instant.

Five modules sitting next to main dot py work, but they are loose files with common names. A module called report could clash with any other report on Ana's machine. The answer is a package: a folder of modules with an underscore underscore init file, imported under one name. The explorer shows it: expense underscore tracker, holding every module. Notice the name. The project, the folder on disk, the command we will install later, are all expense hyphen tracker. But the package is expense underscore tracker, because a Python name cannot contain a hyphen. The REPL shows what happens if you try: import expense minus tracker is read as a subtraction, and Python reports a syntax error. Inside the package, modules import each other with a leading dot, which means: from this package. Even lazy imports work that way. The command loop moved into a file with a special name, underscore underscore main underscore underscore dot py, inside a function called main. python dash m expense underscore tracker runs that file, and the terminal shows it working: recent seven, the same answer as before. At the bottom of the file is a guard you will see in almost every Python program: if underscore underscore name equals main. When the file is run, its name is main and the guard calls main. When it is imported, the name is different, and nothing starts. The diagram shows the two ways in. Python dash m runs the module directly, and main dot py, now three lines long, imports main and calls it, so the habit Ana has from the first course still works.

An interactive prompt is pleasant for exploring, but most tools are run as a single command: the command name, then what to do, then the details, like git commit or pip install. Python's standard library builds that kind of interface with argparse, and the new cli module uses it. parser describes the language. Each command is a sub parser with its own arguments: add takes an amount, a category and an optional note; report takes an optional month, written with two dashes, defaulting to this month; recent takes a number of days, and type equals int converts it. argparse also writes the help and the error messages for free. The diagram follows one real run. The words after the command arrive in sys dot argv. parse args turns them into a namespace, an object whose attributes are the command and its arguments: command report, month twenty twenty six, oh nine. run is a match on the command, and calls report for September. In the terminal, the September report appears: food at sixteen percent, bills at twenty seven. Each run is now a complete, short program: load, do one thing, and save if anything changed, which is why run returns True when it modified the expenses. And add with twelve comma fifty is still refused, by the same parse amount from the decisions course. The interactive loop and its match statement have gone: a command line does the same job with less code, and it can be scripted, scheduled, or run from another program.

Time to step back and look at what has been built. This is the map of the app, and the parts drawn lit are the ones you have written. On the left, the inputs: Ana's bank exports, two months of them in two different encodings, and Ana herself, typing commands. In the middle, the package, six modules, each tagged with the course that built it. money parses amounts, from the decisions course. store and bank read files, JSON and CSV, and validate every row. categorise and report turn rows into understanding. And cli gives it all a command line. On the right is a real run, end to end, starting from a data file holding only the eight expenses Ana typed by hand. Import reads both exports, rejects the same five rows for the same five reasons, and imports twelve, already categorised. Report prints October against the budgets: fun at a hundred and sixty percent, transport careful at ninety six. Recurring finds Netflix and the water bill. Everything on this screen uses only Python's standard library, and you have seen every line of it written. That is a working tool, and it is where many Python tutorials stop. The row along the bottom is still unlit, and it is what separates a script that works today from software that keeps working. The app still stores expenses as anonymous tuples, nothing tests it, it cannot handle the euros, and it can only be run from this folder. The rest of the course fixes all four, starting with the biggest change: giving the app's ideas their own types.

Since the course on holding data, an expense has been a tuple, and the code has been full of e two and e three, numbers you have to remember mean the amount and the category. This course gives the app's ideas their own types, starting with the most important one. A class is a blueprint for a kind of object. The new models module defines Expense, and its underscore underscore init method runs every time an expense is created. Its first parameter, self, is the new object itself, and init stores the four fields on it as attributes. The diagram on the right shows what exists after one expense is made. The name e refers to an instance, an object that holds its own data: the date, the description, the amount and the category. The instance knows its class, and the class holds the code, here just init. Every module now uses attributes: e dot amount instead of e two, e dot category instead of e three. The second table shows the translation. In the terminal, top works exactly as before, which is the point of a refactor: the behaviour stays, the code gets clearer. Then the REPL shows two weaknesses of a plain class. Printing an expense shows only its type and a memory address, nothing useful. And two expenses with identical fields are not equal, because by default, two objects are only equal if they are the very same object. You could fix both by writing more methods, and for years, that is what Python programmers did. The next section shows the modern way.

A class whose main job is to hold some fields is so common that Python has a decorator for it: dataclass. The new Expense is shorter than the old one. It lists its four fields with annotations: a name, a colon, and a type, such as date colon str. That is all. The dataclass decorator reads those annotations and writes the methods for you, as the diagram shows: an init that takes the four fields in order, a repr that prints them by name, and an eq that compares two expenses field by field. The REPL repeats the experiment from the last section. Now printing an expense shows its date, description, amount and category. And two expenses with the same fields are equal, True. A word about annotations, because you will see them everywhere from now on. They document what type each field should hold, but Python itself does not enforce them. Notice that the REPL happily accepted four point five, a float, where the annotation says Decimal. Annotations are for readers, and for tools that check them, which the next course introduces. Nothing outside models dot py had to change. The terminal runs top again and gets the same answer, because every other module only used the attributes, and the dataclass provides exactly the same attributes. That is the quiet strength of the change you made in the last section: once code talks about e dot amount, how an expense is built can change freely. Next, the field that is still just a string.

A category is still a plain string, and a string can be anything. Typing fod instead of food would have created a brand new category, quietly, with no budget. The set of categories is fixed, and Python's way to say so is an enumeration. Category is a StrEnum, with seven members: food, transport, fun, rent, bills, shopping and other. Each member has a name, in capitals, and a value, the string. The diagram shows what Category called with a piece of text does. Food becomes Category dot FOOD, fun becomes Category dot FUN, and fod is not a member at all, so it raises an error. StrEnum has a useful property: each member also is a string. The REPL shows Category dot FOOD equals the string food, True, so saving to JSON, printing, and comparing with text all keep working. And asking whether fod is in Category says False. The rest of the app now uses members instead of strings. The categorisation rules return Category members. The budgets are keyed by them. categorise checks for Category dot OTHER using is, because each member is a single object, like None. And on the command line, add converts its category argument with Category, offering the valid choices. In the terminal, adding a bakery visit to fod is refused by argparse before the app even starts, with the list of real categories in the error. Wherever a value can only be one of a few known things, an enum turns a whole class of typos into errors you see at once.

The import code already refuses negative amounts, but nothing stops some other part of the code from building an expense of minus three directly. A rule that must always hold for every object of a class is called an invariant, and the best place to enforce it is where the object is made. Dataclasses offer a hook for exactly this: a method named underscore underscore post init. The generated init stores the fields, then calls post init, where the class can check them. The diagram follows the two possible outcomes. If the amount is more than zero, you get an expense, and every expense that exists is therefore valid. If not, post init raises InvalidAmount, and no expense is created at all. The REPL tries it with minus three, and the traceback shows the path: through the generated init, into post init, and the error, must be more than zero. The second new idea is a property. Reports keep asking which month an expense is in, which means slicing the date string everywhere. The month method is marked with at property, which lets callers read it like an attribute, e dot month, with no brackets, while it is computed from the date each time. The report now asks expense dot month equals month, which reads like the question it is. A property lets you change how a value is stored without changing a single caller: if the date became a real date object later, only the property would change. Invariants and properties are how a class takes responsibility for its own data, so the rest of the program does not have to.

An amount on its own is not quite money: forty eight means something different in pounds and in euros, and Ana's October export has a payment in euros that the app still rejects. So money gets its own type. Money is a dataclass with two fields, an amount and a currency, and two options: frozen, which makes it impossible to change after it is made, and order, which lets two amounts be compared. Money is a value object. Like a number, it has no identity: two Moneys with the same amount and currency are equal and interchangeable, and because they never change, they are safe to share and can be used as dictionary keys. Then come the methods that make Money behave like a number. underscore underscore add adds two amounts, but only in the same currency: the REPL adds four fifty and twelve ninety nine, and gets a new Money of seventeen forty nine. Neither operand changed; the diagram shows the new object. Adding euros to pounds raises a ValueError, cannot add EUR to GBP, which is exactly the mistake this type exists to catch. underscore underscore radd makes the built in sum work, because sum starts from zero. And underscore underscore format passes a format specification to the amount, so the report's f strings did not change at all. Expense dot amount is now a Money, the stores save the currency alongside the amount, and the defaultdict in the report starts every total at Money of zero. When the app learns to fetch exchange rates, it will convert a Money from one currency to another, and nothing else will need to know.

Python's built in containers, lists and dicts and sets, all support the same few operations: len, a for loop, in, and square brackets. None of that is magic reserved for built ins. Each operation calls a method with a double underscore name, sometimes called a dunder, and any class that defines those methods gets the same syntax. The diagram maps them: len calls underscore underscore len, a for loop calls underscore underscore iter, in calls underscore underscore contains, and square brackets call underscore underscore getitem. The budgets were a frozendict; now they are a Budget, a class that keeps its limits private, in an attribute whose name starts with an underscore, the Python convention for this is internal. Budget defines exactly those four methods, each a single line that asks the frozendict inside. The REPL treats BUDGET like any container. len says six categories. Category dot FUN in BUDGET is True, and Category dot OTHER in BUDGET is False, because other has no budget. Square brackets give fun's limit, sixty. And a list comprehension loops over it, giving the category names in order. The report's code barely changed: it still sorts the budget's categories and looks each limit up, and it cannot tell that it is no longer talking to a dict. Why bother, when a frozendict worked? Because Budget now has a home for budget rules: a monthly limit, a yearly one, a category that carries over. Behaviour has a place to live, behind an interface everyone already knows.

The app raises several kinds of error, InvalidAmount, InvalidRow, and now an unknown category, and each one was defined wherever it was first needed. Code that wants to handle all of them has to list them all. Inheritance fixes that. A class can be based on another class, inheriting everything it has and adding or changing what it needs, and the new errors module puts the app's errors in one family. TrackerError is the parent: something the app refuses to do, with a reason it can print. InvalidAmount, InvalidRow and UnknownCategory all inherit from it, as the diagram shows. InvalidAmount inherits from two classes, TrackerError and ValueError, so code that catches either one catches it. UnknownCategory shows the other half of inheritance. Its init takes the text that failed, calls super dot init with a full message, which runs the parent's init, then keeps the text as an attribute. Category gains a class method, parse, which turns any capitalisation into a member, or raises UnknownCategory. The command line now catches TrackerError, one except clause for the whole family. In the terminal, fod is refused as an unknown category, twelve comma fifty as not a number, and FOOD in capitals is accepted, as food. The REPL prints InvalidAmount's method resolution order, the order Python searches the classes for a method: InvalidAmount, TrackerError, ValueError, and up to object, the root of every class in Python. A shared base class is the simplest, most useful kind of inheritance: it gives a group of things one name to be handled by.

JSON is fine for a few hundred expenses, but a real database is better for years of them, and Python ships with one: SQLite, in the sqlite3 module, a whole database in a single file. The interesting question is how the app can support both without an if statement in every function. The answer is to describe what a store does, not what it is. The store module now has a Protocol called Store, with two methods, load and save, whose bodies are three dots. A protocol is a promise about shape: any object that has these methods counts as a Store, without inheriting from anything. Two classes keep that promise. JsonStore reads and writes the JSON file, as before. SqliteStore creates a table if it does not exist, selects every row to load, and deletes and inserts every row to save, with question marks in the SQL that sqlite3 fills in safely. The table in the middle shows the same two methods doing different work. This is polymorphism: one call, many forms. The command line gains a store option, picks a class from a dictionary, and calls load and save without knowing which store it has. In the terminal, the import runs against SQLite, with the same five rejections, top reads the database, and listing the data folder shows the new database file beside the JSON one. Python calls this duck typing: if it loads like a store and saves like a store, it is a store. The Protocol writes that idea down, so that people, and the type checker you will meet next, know exactly what a store must do.

Saving to SQLite deletes every row and then inserts them again. If the program failed between those two steps, Ana would lose everything. Databases solve this with transactions: a group of changes that either all happen, committed, or none happen, rolled back. Python's with statement is the natural way to express that, and you have used it since the files course. Any class with two methods, underscore underscore enter and underscore underscore exit, can be used with with, and SqliteStore now is one. Enter opens the connection, makes sure the table exists, and returns the store. Exit is called when the block ends, however it ends, and Python tells it whether an exception happened. No error: commit. An error: roll back. Either way: close the connection. Exit returns False, which means the error is not swallowed; it carries on to whoever handles it. The diagram shows the two paths. The REPL tests the dangerous one. The database starts with twelve expenses, imported before the session. Then a with block saves an empty list, which deletes everything, and then divides by zero, a stand in for any crash. suppress, a context manager from the standard library, swallows the ZeroDivisionError outside our store, so the REPL keeps going.
