And the database still has twelve expenses: the delete was rolled back. JsonStore gains an enter and an exit that do nothing, so both stores still have the same shape, and the command line now opens whichever store it uses in a with block. The app's ideas are now types: Expense, Category, Money, Budget, a family of errors and two stores. Next, we make sure they keep working.

A program that works today can break tomorrow, when someone changes one module and forgets another depends on it. This course adds the tools that catch that, starting with types. You met annotations in the dataclass. Now every function in the package has them: what each parameter should be, and what it returns, after an arrow. The diagram shows report as nothing but its types: a list of expenses and a month string in, nothing out. Python ignores these hints when it runs. A separate tool, mypy, reads them and checks that the whole program agrees with itself, without running it. The project now has a pyproject dot toml, the standard file describing a Python project. It names the project, the Python it needs, and a group of development tools, pinned to exact versions so every machine gets the same ones: mypy, pytest and ruff. pip install dash dash group dev installs them into the project's own environment, the one from the very first section. Then mypy runs, and it finds something real: two errors on line eighty of cli dot py. The object it is opening with with has no enter and no exit method. Why? STORES holds two classes, JsonStore and SqliteStore, and mypy has to describe that dictionary with a single type. They share no base class, so it falls back to the only thing they have in common: object. The program runs perfectly, so no test would ever have noticed. But the protocol written in the last course, the promise that both are stores, is not connected to anything. The fix is one annotation, and the next section makes it.

The first line of this step is the fix mypy asked for: STORES is annotated as a dict from strings to types of Store. Run mypy again, and it reports no issues in ten files. The protocol from the last course now protects the command line: a store missing a method would be an error before the program ever runs. Types check that the pieces fit. Tests check that they do the right thing, and pytest is how most Python projects write them. A test is a plain function whose name starts with test, in a file whose name starts with test, inside the tests folder. The diagram follows one. It calls the code under test, adding four fifty to twelve ninety nine, and then asserts what must be true: the total equals seventeen forty nine. If the assertion holds, the test passes. If it does not, pytest shows both values and exactly where they differ. Errors are tested too. pytest dot raises is a context manager that passes only if the code inside it raises the expected error, with a matching message: adding euros to pounds must fail, and twelve comma fifty must not be a number. The categorise tests pin down two of the rules: an Amazon payment is shopping, an unknown shop is other. In the terminal, pytest finds six tests in two files and runs them all, each dot a pass. Tests are also documentation that cannot go out of date. Anyone can read these six names and know what the money type promises, and if a change ever breaks a promise, the test with that name will fail.

The bank import has five ways to reject a row, and writing five almost identical tests would be dull to write and dull to read. pytest has two features that keep tests short. The first is parametrisation. One test function, test a bad row is refused, is decorated with a list of cases. Each case is a change to an otherwise good row, and the reason the app should give. GOOD, at the top, is a real row from Ana's October export, and GOOD with a vertical bar and a change merges the two dicts: a good row with one field broken. pytest runs the function once per case, as the diagram shows, and names each run after its data, so the collect only listing in the terminal reads like a specification: not a number, no date, more than zero, needs a rate. The second feature is the fixture. validate needs a set of rows it has already seen, and every test needs a fresh, empty one, or one test's rows would leak into the next. The fixture called seen makes one. Any test that names a parameter seen gets a new set, created just for it. Fixtures are how tests share setup without sharing state. Two more tests complete the file: a good row is categorised as food, and the same row twice is a duplicate, which uses the fixture's memory deliberately. In the terminal, pytest dash q runs everything: twelve tests, all passing. Every rejection the app printed in the course on importing is now a line of data in a test, so none of them can quietly disappear.

The command line is harder to test than a function. It loads from a file, saves to a file, and prints. A test that touched Ana's real data would be slow, would leave files behind, and would fail on any machine where the data is different. The protocol from the classes course pays off here. Anything with enter, exit, load and save is a store, so a test can use a fake one: FakeStore, which keeps the expenses in memory and records whatever it was asked to save. pytest's monkeypatch fixture swaps it in, replacing STORES of json with a function that returns the fake, for the length of one test, and then puts the real one back. The diagram shows main calling the same methods either way; the dashed arrow is the store it would have used. The first test runs the real main with add three twenty food bakery, then checks two things: the fake received exactly one new expense, the bakery, and capsys, another fixture, captured exactly the line main printed. The second test checks the opposite: a refused amount saves nothing at all. The third uses monkeypatch on a different kind of thing: the course's fixed today, set to the tenth of October, so that recent can be tested against dates that will never change. In the terminal, the three new tests pass, and then all fifteen. Only fake what crosses the edge of your program: files, the network, the clock. Here, everything inside the package runs for real, and only the store is pretended.

The import has been printing its rejections, and that mixes two different kinds of output: answers Ana asked for, and details about how the app got there. Python's logging module is built for the second kind. Each module gets its own logger, named after the module, here expense tracker dot bank. bank now logs each rejected row as a warning, and store logs at debug level how many expenses it loaded and from where. Nothing is printed directly. Where the messages go is decided once, in cli dot main, by basicConfig. It sets the level, the least important message to show, and the format: the level, the logger's name, and the message. By default the level is warning. With the new dash v flag it is debug, and everything shows. The diagram follows one message from the logger, through the level check, to the handler, which writes to standard error. In the terminal, the import's last lines are warnings, each naming the logger it came from, and zero were imported, because Ana's data already contains every good row. Then dash v top shows a debug line, loaded twenty expenses, before the answer. Notice the arguments in the log calls. The message has percent placeholders, and the values are passed separately. Logging only builds the final string if the message is actually shown, so debug messages cost almost nothing when they are off. And because logs go to standard error, a report redirected to a file stays clean. pytest still passes all fifteen tests: logging changed what the app says, not what it does.

It would be useful to know how long the report and the import take, but adding timing code inside them would bury what they do. A decorator adds behaviour around a function without touching its code, and you have used several: dataclass, property, the pytest fixture. The new timing module writes one. timed takes a function and returns a new function, wrapper, which notes the time, calls the original with whatever arguments it was given, and logs how long it took, even if it raised. The at sign is shorthand: writing at timed above def report means report equals timed of report. The name report now refers to the wrapper. The diagram shows what makes this work: a closure. When timed returns, its local variable function would normally disappear. But wrapper uses it, so Python keeps it in a closure cell attached to wrapper, and every call to report goes through the wrapper to the original stored there. functools dot wraps copies the original's name and docstring onto the wrapper, so it still looks like report, and keeps a link to it in under under wrapped, which the terminal prints. The square brackets after timed declare type parameters, so that mypy knows the wrapper takes exactly the arguments the original did and returns the same type. In the terminal, dash v report prints the table, followed by a debug line: report took a fraction of a millisecond, on this machine, with CPython three fifteen one. Timings like that vary from run to run, so treat them as a rough guide, not a promise. That question, how fast, and why, is what the next course is about.

Since the course on importing, one row of Ana's October export has been refused: forty eight euros, spent in Porto, because the app had no exchange rate. Rates change every day, so they come from a service, over HTTP, the protocol behind every web page and almost every API. This course's service is a stand in, stub slash rates server dot py, built only from Python's standard library. It answers on this machine, takes a fifth of a second like a real service across the internet, and always gives the same rates, so every run of the course agrees. The new rates module asks it. rate builds the address, slash rates slash EUR, and urlopen sends a GET request and returns the response, which is JSON, read with the same json module as the save course. The diagram follows one round trip: the request, the service, and the reply, with the rate as a string, so it becomes an exact Decimal. If the service has no rate, it replies with the status code four oh four, which urllib raises as an HTTPError, and rate turns into the app's own error, NoRate. to gbp multiplies an amount by its rate and rounds to the penny. And validate, in the bank module, now converts every row to pounds instead of refusing foreign ones. In the terminal, one euro is eighty six pence, XYZ has no rate, and the import finally brings in the Porto row, as forty one twenty eight in pounds. One test had to change with it: the bank test that expected euros to be refused now checks that forty eight euros become forty one twenty eight pounds, with rate replaced by monkeypatch, so the tests never touch the network. All fifteen pass. The network is the slowest thing this app touches, by far. The next section shows how much that matters, and what to do about it.

Ana's next trip takes in five currencies, and the rates command asks for all of them. Asked one by one, five requests take five times as long as one, and the terminal shows about a second, almost all of it spent waiting for replies. Waiting is not work. A program waiting for the network could be waiting for four other replies at the same time. That is what asyncio is for. rates at once is an async function, written async def, and it builds five tasks, one per currency. urllib itself blocks while it waits, so asyncio dot to thread runs each request in a worker thread, and gather starts all five at once and waits until every one has finished, returning the results in the order they were asked. The diagram shows the event loop, the scheduler at the heart of asyncio, with five tasks, each suspended while it waits for its reply. When a task reaches await, it gives control back to the loop, which runs whichever task can make progress. The command line starts all of this with asyncio dot run. In the terminal, the same five rates arrive in about a fifth of a second: the five waits overlapped instead of adding up. The plot puts the two runs side by side. Those timings are this machine's, on this run, and they will vary; what does not vary is the shape, five waits in the time of one. asyncio shines when a program spends its time waiting: on the network, on a database, on many clients at once. Whether that is your program's problem is a question you answer by measuring, which is the next section.

When a program feels slow, the tempting move is to guess which part is slow and rewrite it. The guess is usually wrong. Python ships a profiler, cProfile, which records how long every function call takes, and the rule is: measure first. The new bench folder holds measurements that the app itself never imports. year dot py makes up a year of bank rows, sixty thousand of them, the same on every run because its random generator is seeded. profile import turns the profiler on, validates every row, turns it off, and then asks pstats, the profiler's statistics, for each function's own time: the time spent in that function itself, not in the functions it called. The terminal shows the result on this machine. The whole year took under half a second. validate's own work is the biggest share, about a third. Then come the regular expression searches, categorising, hashing the duplicate check's keys, parsing amounts, and the Expense invariant. The plot draws those shares. Read what that says. There is no single slow line, and a year of rows takes less time than one request to the rate service. Rewriting validate to be twice as fast would save a fraction of a second a year. That is the most common result of measuring, and the most useful: it tells you what not to spend your time on. The slow part of this app is not its Python, it is its waiting. To tell those two kinds of slow apart, there is one simple question, and the next section asks it.

Before choosing a tool to make a program faster, ask where its time goes: is it computing, or is it waiting? Code that spends its time computing is called CPU bound. Code that spends it waiting for input and output, a disk, a network, a database, is called I O bound. Python can tell you which. time dot perf counter is a clock on the wall, measuring how long something took. time dot process time counts only the processor time this process actually used. where time goes measures two jobs both ways. The terminal shows the answer. Five rates, one by one, took about a second on the wall clock, but only a few hundredths of a second of processor time. Nearly all of it was waiting: I O bound. Categorising sixty thousand descriptions took the same small amount on both clocks: every moment of it was computing, CPU bound. The plot shows the two bars per job. A large gap between wall and CPU time means waiting; no gap means working. The table below is the decision this course builds towards. For waiting, overlap the waits: asyncio, as in the last section, or threads, which also work well because a waiting thread does not need the processor. For computing, you need more processors working at once. In standard Python, that has meant processes. And in Python three point fifteen, there is a second option, which needs a picture of its own: the global interpreter lock, and the build of Python that removes it.

This picture explains one of Python's most famous limitations, and the newest way around it. On the left is the Python you have used all along. Inside CPython, the global interpreter lock, the GIL, is a single lock that a thread must hold to run Python code. Four threads can exist at once, but only the one holding the lock runs Python; the others wait. That made CPython's internals simple and single threaded code fast, at a price: threads cannot use more than one core for Python work. For waiting, that does not matter, because a thread releases the lock while it waits for the network. For computing, it does. On the right is the free threaded build, python three point fifteen t. It has no global lock. Threads run Python code on different cores at the same time, and the objects they share protect themselves with small locks of their own, only when needed. The terminal panel shows Python's own answers, on both builds: sys dot underscore is gil enabled is True on the standard build and False on the free threaded one, and the build configuration says the same. This machine has four cores. The table lists the trade. The free threaded build was experimental in three thirteen and is supported since three fourteen. Its single threaded code runs a little slower, which the next section measures, and in exchange threads doing CPU work can run in parallel. It is a separate build you choose to install, not a switch, and code written for the standard build runs on it unchanged. Whether it helps your program is, once again, something to measure. That is next.

Here is the measurement: the same CPU bound job, categorising a year of descriptions twenty times over, done on one thread and then split across four, on both builds of Python three fifteen one. threads dot py splits the list into four chunks and hands them to a ThreadPoolExecutor, the standard library's ready made pool of worker threads, then times the whole thing. The very same file runs on both builds, because the package uses only the standard library. The terminal shows two runs of each. With the GIL on, four threads take as long as one, about a second, and sometimes a little longer: the threads take turns, and taking turns has a cost. On the free threaded build, one thread is a little slower than on the standard build, the price the last picture mentioned, and four threads are faster, by roughly one and a half times in these runs. The plot draws the first run of each, and the table lists both runs' speed ups. Two honest observations. First, the gain is real, but it is not four times, even with four cores. This course does not measure why, and the reasons vary with the machine and the workload, so the only safe statement is what was measured: on this machine, about one and a half. Second, the numbers move from run to run. Never trust a single timing. Run it several times, on the machine that matters, and look at the spread. If the free threaded build fits your workload, it lets threads do CPU work in Python for the first time. If not, there is the older answer, next.

Before free threading, the standard answer to CPU bound Python was processes, and it is still the most dependable one. A process is a separate running program, with its own memory and its own Python interpreter, and so its own GIL. Four processes can run Python on four cores at the same time, on the ordinary build. processes dot py does the same work as the threads benchmark, but with a ProcessPoolExecutor. The code is almost identical, which is the point of concurrent dot futures: threads and processes share one interface. There is one important difference, drawn in the diagram. Processes do not share memory, so each chunk of descriptions is pickled, turned into bytes, sent to a worker, and the results are sent back the same way. That copying is the cost of processes, and it is why they suit big chunks of independent work, not lots of tiny tasks. Notice the if name equals main guard at the bottom: on some systems, each worker process starts by importing this file, and the guard stops each of them from starting a pool of its own. The terminal shows two runs on the standard build: four processes were roughly three times faster than one, more than threads managed on either build, and again the exact numbers vary between runs. The table sums up the choice. Processes need no special build and scale with cores, but copy their data and start slowly. Threads share memory and start fast, and need the free threaded build to compute in parallel. The app can now talk to the network and knows where its time goes. One thing remains: getting it out of this folder and onto other machines.

Software that leaves its author's machine needs settings that can change without editing code: which store to use, where the data lives. A well behaved program reads them from several places, and the rule for which one wins must be simple. The diagram is that rule. First come the built in defaults. A settings file overrides them. The environment overrides the file. And a flag on the command line overrides everything, for that one run. The new config module implements exactly that, in one function. It starts from the defaults, reads expense tracker dot toml with tomllib, the standard library's TOML reader, then checks environment variables starting with EXPENSE underscore TRACKER, then the flags. It returns every setting together with where it came from, because the most common configuration question is not what is the value, but why. A new command, config, prints the answer. In the terminal, with nothing extra, the store is json, from the toml file. With EXPENSE TRACKER STORE set to sqlite in the environment, it is sqlite, and the output says so. Add dash dash store json as well, and the flag wins. The stores now take their path from the data setting, so the Protocol gained an init, and the fake in the tests takes a path too. Two new tests pin the precedence down, and all seventeen pass. One more rule, from the module's docstring: secrets, such as an API key, belong in the environment, never in a file, because files end up in version control, and version control is forever.

So far, expense tracker runs only from inside its own folder, with python dash m. Shipping it means turning it into a package that pip can install anywhere, with a command of its own. All of that is described in pyproject dot toml, which gains three things, highlighted in the editor. A build system: setuptools, which pip downloads into a temporary environment just to build the package. A script: the command expense hyphen tracker, which runs the main function in the cli module, the same function python dash m has called all along. And the list of packages to include: expense underscore tracker, but not the bench, the stub or the tests. The version is now one point oh. In the terminal, pip wheel builds a wheel, the standard file format for a built Python package, into the dist folder. The table reads its name: the project, version one point oh point oh, py3 for any Python three, and none any, because it contains no compiled code and runs on any platform. Then the real test of a package: a brand new virtual environment, created in the home folder, with nothing in it. pip installs the wheel into it, and that environment now has its own expense tracker command. Running it prints October's report, using the installed copy of the package, not the files in the project. This is the same journey every library on the Python Package Index makes, and publishing to it is one more command away. One name, expense tracker with a hyphen, now really is everywhere: the folder, the project, the wheel and the command.

Ana would like to add expenses from her phone, and a phone talks to a web API: a program that answers HTTP requests with JSON. You built the other side of this in the last course, when the app asked the rate service for rates. Now the app is the service. The new api module uses http dot server, the same standard library server the rate stub uses. Its handler has a method for each kind of request. do GET answers slash report, with what was spent in a month, by category, as JSON. do POST answers slash expenses: it reads the JSON body, checks the amount with parse amount and the category with Category dot parse, exactly as the command line does, then loads, appends and saves through the JSON store. The diagram follows one POST through those steps. Every answer carries an HTTP status code: two hundred for a good read, two oh one for something created, four hundred for a bad request, four oh four for an unknown address. A new command, serve, starts the server; in this section it is already running in the background. The terminal uses curl, a standard command line HTTP client. September's report comes back as JSON. Adding a bakery visit returns two oh one, added. Twelve comma fifty returns four hundred, with the same error message the command line gives. An unknown page returns four oh four. And listing food from the command line shows the bakery, added over the web. For real traffic, a framework such as FastAPI adds routing, validation and documentation, and the last section points there. The point here is that the API is not a second app: it is one more way into the same Money, Category and store.

Everything in this course used Python's standard library, on purpose: it ships with every Python, it never goes out of date, and it shows how things really work. Out in the world, each part of expense tracker has a well known tool that does the same job at a bigger scale, and now you know what each of those tools is for. The diagram pairs them up. The command line, built with argparse, is the job of Typer or Click. The web API, built on http dot server, is the job of FastAPI or Django, which add routing, validation and documentation. The stores, JSON and SQLite, grow into PostgreSQL, often reached through SQLAlchemy. The rows of a CSV, walked with loops and generators, become data frames in pandas or Polars, which do the grouping and summing of the report course in a single line. Packaging with pip, venv and pyproject is what uv makes fast, and what PyPI distributes. And one highlighted line goes further than the rest. A year of one person's expenses fits on one machine. A year of a whole bank's transactions does not. Processing data at that scale, across many machines, is the job of PySpark and Databricks, and that is where the next series begins, with the same habits you learned here: real data, real output, one step at a time. Whichever direction you take, the Python underneath is the Python you now know: names and objects, functions and classes, exceptions, generators, and the standard library.
